title: NEC Article 240 — Overcurrent Protection
description: Fuses, circuit breakers, conductor protection, and overcurrent device sizing per NEC 2023 Article 240. 30 questions.

questions.question: According to NEC 240.4, what is the general rule for overcurrent protection of conductors?
choices: Conductors shall be protected at their rated voltage
Conductors shall be protected so that the overcurrent device rating does not exceed the conductor ampacity
Conductors shall be protected at the next-higher standard overcurrent device rating above their ampacity
Conductors shall be protected only when supplying loads over 15 amperes
questions.answer: Conductors shall be protected so that the overcurrent device rating does not exceed the conductor ampacity
questions.explanation: NEC 240.4 establishes the general rule that conductors shall be protected against overcurrent in accordance with their ampacities. The overcurrent protective device (OCPD) rating shall not exceed the ampacity of the conductor it protects, subject to the specific exceptions listed in 240.4(A) through (G).

questions.question: Under NEC 240.4(B), which of the following is a condition that must be met to use the next-higher standard overcurrent device rating above a conductor's ampacity?
choices: The conductor must be rated for 90°C insulation
The overcurrent device rating must not exceed 800 amperes
The load must be purely resistive
The conductor must be copper only
questions.answer: The overcurrent device rating must not exceed 800 amperes
questions.explanation: NEC 240.4(B) permits the next-higher standard overcurrent device rating (above the conductor's ampacity) only when: (1) the conductor ampacity does not correspond to a standard rating of an overcurrent device, (2) the overcurrent device rating does not exceed 800 amperes, and (3) the overcurrent device does not supply more than one receptacle for portable cord-and-plug-connected equipment.

questions.question: Per NEC 240.4(D), what is the maximum overcurrent protection permitted for 12 AWG copper conductors?
choices: 15 amperes
20 amperes
25 amperes
30 amperes
questions.answer: 20 amperes
questions.explanation: NEC 240.4(D) establishes maximum overcurrent protection for small conductors. 12 AWG copper conductors are limited to 20 amperes, 14 AWG copper is limited to 15 amperes, and 10 AWG copper is limited to 30 amperes, regardless of the conductor's listed ampacity at higher temperature ratings.

questions.question: Which of the following lists represents the standard ampere ratings for fuses and inverse time circuit breakers as specified in NEC 240.6(A)?
questions.explanation: NEC 240.6(A) lists the standard ampere ratings for fuses and inverse time circuit breakers, which include: 15, 20, 25, 30, 35, 40, 45, 50, 60, 70, 80, 90, 100, 110, 125, 150, 175, 200, 225, 250, 300, 350, 400, 450, 500, 600, 700, 800, 1000, 1200, 1600, 2000, 2500, 3000, 4000, 5000, and 6000 amperes. These standard ratings govern when the next-higher rule of 240.4(B) applies.

questions.question: Per NEC 240.10, which statement correctly describes supplementary overcurrent protection?
choices: It is permitted to serve as the sole branch-circuit overcurrent protection and must be readily accessible
It is not a substitute for branch-circuit overcurrent protection and is not required to be readily accessible
It must be rated at least equal to the branch-circuit overcurrent device
It must be installed in the same enclosure as the branch-circuit overcurrent device
questions.answer: It is not a substitute for branch-circuit overcurrent protection and is not required to be readily accessible
questions.explanation: NEC 240.10 states that supplementary overcurrent protection (such as in luminaires, appliances, or other equipment) is not a substitute for required branch-circuit overcurrent protective devices and shall not be used as the sole overcurrent protection for branch-circuit conductors. Additionally, supplementary overcurrent protective devices are not required to be readily accessible.

questions.question: NEC 240.15(A) requires that a fuse or overcurrent trip unit of a circuit breaker be connected in series with each ungrounded conductor. What alternative method is specifically permitted?
choices: A ground-fault circuit interrupter (GFCI) on each circuit
An arc-fault circuit interrupter (AFCI) on each phase
A current transformer with a trip coil relay as the overcurrent unit
A thermal cutout device installed in the load equipment
questions.answer: A current transformer with a trip coil relay as the overcurrent unit
questions.explanation: NEC 240.15(A) requires a fuse or overcurrent trip unit of a circuit breaker to be connected in series with each ungrounded conductor. A current transformer (CT) with a trip coil and relay is specifically permitted as an alternative overcurrent unit for providing the required protection in series with each ungrounded conductor.

questions.question: According to NEC 240.20, which conductor is generally NOT required to be opened by an overcurrent device?
choices: An ungrounded (hot) conductor in a single-phase circuit
An ungrounded (hot) conductor in a three-phase circuit
The grounded (neutral) conductor
The equipment grounding conductor
questions.answer: The grounded (neutral) conductor
questions.explanation: NEC 240.20 requires that each ungrounded conductor of a circuit be protected by an overcurrent device. The grounded conductor (neutral) is generally not opened or interrupted by an overcurrent device, as interrupting the neutral while the hot conductors remain energized could create dangerous voltage imbalances and is not needed for overcurrent protection of the neutral.

questions.question: NEC 240.21 requires that the overcurrent protective device be located at the point where a conductor receives its supply. What does this section also provide?
choices: Exceptions that allow tap conductors to run unprotected under specific conditions listed in 240.21(A) through (H)
A requirement that all conductors be protected within 10 feet of the source
A blanket exemption for conductors over 4 AWG
Permission to omit overcurrent protection on any service conductor
questions.answer: Exceptions that allow tap conductors to run unprotected under specific conditions listed in 240.21(A) through (H)
questions.explanation: NEC 240.21 states that overcurrent protection shall be provided at the point where a conductor receives its supply. However, it also provides specific tap conductor exceptions in 240.21(A) through (H) that allow conductors to run without overcurrent protection at their supply end under defined conditions (such as the 10-foot tap, 25-foot tap, and outdoor tap rules), so long as prescribed sizing and termination requirements are met.

questions.question: Under the 10-foot indoor tap rule in NEC 240.21(B)(1), the tap conductor ampacity must be at least what fraction of the rating of the overcurrent device protecting the feeder?
choices: 1/3 of the feeder OCPD rating
1/4 of the feeder OCPD rating
1/10 of the feeder OCPD rating
Equal to the feeder OCPD rating
questions.answer: 1/10 of the feeder OCPD rating
questions.explanation: NEC 240.21(B)(1) permits a 10-foot indoor tap provided the tap conductor has an ampacity of at least 1/10 (one-tenth) the rating of the overcurrent device protecting the feeder conductors, the tap terminates in a single circuit breaker or set of fuses that will limit the load, the tap is not over 10 feet long, and it is in a raceway or protected from physical damage.

questions.question: Under the 25-foot indoor tap rule of NEC 240.21(B)(2), what is the minimum required ampacity of the tap conductor relative to the feeder OCPD?
choices: At least 1/10 of the feeder OCPD rating
At least 1/3 of the feeder OCPD rating
At least 1/2 of the feeder OCPD rating
Equal to or greater than the feeder OCPD rating
questions.answer: At least 1/3 of the feeder OCPD rating
questions.explanation: NEC 240.21(B)(2) permits a tap conductor no more than 25 feet long provided the tap conductor ampacity is not less than 1/3 of the rating of the overcurrent device protecting the feeder, the tap conductor terminates in a single circuit breaker or set of fuses rated at or below the tap conductor ampacity, and the tap conductor is protected from physical damage and installed in a raceway.

questions.question: Per NEC 240.24(A), overcurrent protective devices must be readily accessible. What is the maximum height for the center of the operating handle of an overcurrent device in its highest position?
choices: 5 feet 6 inches above the floor or working platform
6 feet above the floor or working platform
6 feet 7 inches above the floor or working platform
7 feet above the floor or working platform
questions.answer: 6 feet 7 inches above the floor or working platform
questions.explanation: NEC 240.24(A) requires that overcurrent devices be readily accessible, and specifically states that the center of the grip of the operating handle of the circuit breaker or switch, when in its highest position, shall not be more than 6 feet 7 inches (2.0 m) above the floor or working platform. A panel blocked by storage would also violate the readily accessible requirement.

questions.question: NEC 240.24(F) prohibits overcurrent protective devices from being located in which specific area?
choices: In attached garages
Over the steps of a stairway
In unfinished basements
In outdoor weatherproof enclosures
questions.answer: Over the steps of a stairway
questions.explanation: NEC 240.24(F) specifically prohibits overcurrent protective devices from being located in the vicinity of easily ignitable material, and additionally states they shall not be located over the steps of a stairway. This provision prevents a person from having to stand on stairs (an unstable, hazardous position) to operate a panel or reset a breaker.

questions.question: Per NEC 240.51 and 240.54, which statement correctly describes the use of Edison-base fuses?
choices: Edison-base fuses may be installed in new installations where listed for the purpose
Edison-base fuses are for replacement only in existing fuseholders and shall not be used in new installations; Type S adapters are non-removable once installed
Edison-base fuses can be replaced with Type S fuses only when the load exceeds 30 amperes
Edison-base fuses must be replaced with cartridge fuses in all occupancies after 2011
questions.answer: Edison-base fuses are for replacement only in existing fuseholders and shall not be used in new installations; Type S adapters are non-removable once installed
questions.explanation: NEC 240.51 limits Edison-base fuseholders to replacement of existing fuseholders and prohibits them from being installed in new installations. NEC 240.54 requires Type S fuses, adapters, and fuseholders — and specifies that Type S adapters, once inserted into an Edison-base fuseholder, are non-removable, preventing the substitution of an oversized fuse that could defeat overcurrent protection.

questions.question: According to NEC 240.80, what must a circuit breaker clearly indicate?
choices: The date of manufacture and interrupting rating
The open (off), closed (on), and tripped positions of the operating handle
The voltage rating and current rating on the face of the device
The wire gauge range and torque specification for terminals
questions.answer: The open (off), closed (on), and tripped positions of the operating handle
questions.explanation: NEC 240.80 requires that circuit breaker operating handles clearly indicate whether they are in the open (off), closed (on), or tripped position. This allows a person to quickly determine the status of a circuit breaker without having to test the circuit, which is important for both normal operation and safety during electrical emergencies.

questions.question: NEC 240.85 covers series-rated systems. Which of the following statements best describes the field-marking requirement for a series-rated system?
choices: No field marking is required if the equipment was listed by a nationally recognized testing laboratory
The equipment must be marked with a caution label indicating the series combination rating and requiring identified replacement components
The series rating must only be marked on the upstream overcurrent device
Series-rated equipment must be marked with the voltage class and short-circuit current rating only
questions.answer: The equipment must be marked with a caution label indicating the series combination rating and requiring identified replacement components
questions.explanation: NEC 240.85 requires that series-rated systems be tested and listed, and that the electrical equipment be legibly marked in the field with a caution label that includes the series combination rating and states that identified replacement components are required. This ensures that any future maintenance or replacement does not inadvertently compromise the tested series rating of the system.

questions.question: NEC 240.4(E) states that tap conductors shall be protected against overcurrent in accordance with which section?
choices: NEC 240.4(B) — next-higher standard rating rule
NEC 240.21 — overcurrent protection at the point where the tap conductor receives its supply
NEC 240.6(A) — standard ampere ratings only
NEC 240.15(A) — series protection in each ungrounded conductor
questions.answer: NEC 240.21 — overcurrent protection at the point where the tap conductor receives its supply
questions.explanation: NEC 240.4(E) directs that tap conductors shall be protected in accordance with NEC 240.21. Rather than requiring an overcurrent device at the supply end of every tap conductor, 240.21 provides specific conditions under which tap conductors (10-ft, 25-ft, outside, feeder taps, transformer secondary taps, etc.) may run without an OCPD at their point of supply, provided the tap meets the prescribed length, ampacity, and termination requirements.

questions.question: NEC 240.4(G) states that overcurrent protection for motor-circuit conductors shall be provided as specified in which NEC article?
choices: Article 215 — Feeders
Article 310 — Conductors for General Wiring
Article 430 — Motors, Motor Circuits, and Controllers
Article 445 — Generators
questions.answer: Article 430 — Motors, Motor Circuits, and Controllers
questions.explanation: NEC 240.4(G) refers motor-circuit conductor protection to Article 430. Motor circuits are unique because motors have high inrush currents during starting that would trip a standard overcurrent device sized to the conductor ampacity. Article 430 provides specific rules for motor branch-circuit short-circuit and ground-fault protection, motor overload protection, and feeder protection that differ from the general rules in 240.4.

questions.question: Under NEC 240.6(B), when are fuses with non-standard ampere ratings permitted?
choices: Only for motor circuits rated over 100 horsepower
When the non-standard rating is a manufacturer's standard rating recognized by the listing or labeling of the equipment
Only for fuses used as supplementary overcurrent protection inside equipment
When the authority having jurisdiction (AHJ) grants written approval
questions.answer: When the non-standard rating is a manufacturer's standard rating recognized by the listing or labeling of the equipment
questions.explanation: NEC 240.6(B) permits the use of fuses with non-standard ampere ratings where such ratings are recognized as manufacturer's standard ratings and the fuse is listed or labeled for use in a specific piece of equipment. This allows equipment manufacturers to incorporate fuses with intermediate ratings (e.g., 22A or 35A) that are specifically designed and listed for the equipment's protection requirements.

questions.question: Per NEC 240.15(B), in a single-phase, line-to-line load connected to a three-phase system using only two of the three phases, what overcurrent protection is required?
choices: A two-pole overcurrent device protecting both ungrounded conductors supplying the load
A single-pole overcurrent device on one ungrounded conductor only
A three-pole overcurrent device sized for all three phases
No overcurrent device is required if the load is less than 600V
questions.answer: A two-pole overcurrent device protecting both ungrounded conductors supplying the load
questions.explanation: NEC 240.15(B) requires that where a single-phase load is connected line-to-line on a three-phase system, a two-pole overcurrent device shall be used to protect both of the ungrounded conductors supplying that load. This ensures that a fault in either ungrounded conductor is interrupted, and both poles open simultaneously to de-energize the load.

questions.question: Under the outdoor tap rule of NEC 240.21(B)(3), which of the following is a key requirement for outside tap conductors?
choices: The outdoor tap must not exceed 25 feet in length
There is no specified length limit, but the tap must terminate in a single overcurrent device rated at or below the tap conductor ampacity
The outdoor tap must have an ampacity of at least 1/3 of the feeder OCPD rating
The outdoor tap must be installed in rigid metal conduit only
questions.answer: There is no specified length limit, but the tap must terminate in a single overcurrent device rated at or below the tap conductor ampacity
questions.explanation: NEC 240.21(B)(3) allows outside tap conductors (exposed to outdoor weather) to be of unlimited length, provided the conductors are protected from physical damage, terminate in a single circuit breaker or set of fuses with a rating no greater than the tap conductor ampacity, and are not over 100 feet in length (for high-bay warehouse industrial applications this may differ; the general rule for outdoor taps is no specified maximum length as long as requirements are met). The key distinction from indoor taps is the absence of a strict length cap, with the termination in a single OCPD being the critical requirement.

questions.question: NEC 240.21(C) addresses transformer secondary conductors. Under the 10-foot secondary tap rule of NEC 240.21(C)(1), what is the minimum required ampacity of the secondary conductor?
choices: At least 1/10 of the primary overcurrent device rating reflected through the transformer turns ratio

At least equal to the combined computed load of all circuits supplied by the secondary conductors, and the secondary conductors must terminate in a single set of overcurrent devices rated at or below their ampacity
At least 1/3 of the secondary transformer rating
At least equal to the primary conductor ampacity multiplied by the transformer turns ratio
questions.answer: At least equal to the combined computed load of all circuits supplied by the secondary conductors, and the secondary conductors must terminate in a single set of overcurrent devices rated at or below their ampacity
questions.explanation: NEC 240.21(C)(1) permits transformer secondary conductors of up to 10 feet in length without an overcurrent device at the secondary terminals provided: (1) the secondary conductors have an ampacity that, when multiplied by the ratio of secondary-to-primary voltage, is at least 1/10 of the primary overcurrent device rating; (2) the secondary conductors terminate in a single set of overcurrent devices rated at or below the secondary conductor ampacity; and (3) the conductors are protected from physical damage.

questions.question: Per NEC 240.21(D), how are service-entrance conductors protected against overcurrent?
choices: By an overcurrent device located at the utility transformer
By service equipment (the main service disconnect or main breaker) at the service entrance point
By an overcurrent device installed at the meter socket
Service conductors do not require overcurrent protection
questions.answer: By service equipment (the main service disconnect or main breaker) at the service entrance point
questions.explanation: NEC 240.21(D) states that service conductors shall be protected by an overcurrent device at the point where they enter the building or structure — that is, by the service equipment (main service disconnect or main breaker panel). Because no standard overcurrent device is placed between the utility and the service equipment, the service equipment itself provides the overcurrent protection for the service-entrance conductors.

questions.question: NEC 240.24(B) prohibits the installation of overcurrent protective devices in which type of room or area?
choices: Laundry rooms in dwellings
Bathrooms
Mechanical equipment rooms
Attached garages
questions.answer: Bathrooms
questions.explanation: NEC 240.24(B) prohibits overcurrent protective devices from being located in bathrooms of dwelling units, dormitories, hotels, or motels. This prohibition exists because bathrooms contain plumbing and water sources that create increased shock hazards, and the confined space makes it impractical and dangerous to operate electrical panels in such an environment.

questions.question: According to NEC 240.24(C), overcurrent protective devices shall not be located in which area of a dwelling?
choices: Attached garages
Hallways less than 3 feet wide
Clothes closets
Attics without permanent lighting
questions.answer: Clothes closets
questions.explanation: NEC 240.24(C) prohibits overcurrent protective devices from being installed in the area of clothes closets. This restriction prevents the hazard of electrical equipment being located near flammable clothing and fabrics, reducing fire risk in an area where a panel fault or arc could easily ignite stored materials.

questions.question: NEC 240.24(D) addresses overcurrent protective devices where they may be exposed to physical damage. What does this section require?
choices: OCPDs shall be installed in GFCI-protected enclosures when exposed to physical damage
OCPDs shall not be located where they are exposed to physical damage
OCPDs in areas of physical damage must be rated for 125% of the design load
OCPDs must be installed behind a locked cover when exposed to physical damage
questions.answer: OCPDs shall not be located where they are exposed to physical damage
questions.explanation: NEC 240.24(D) requires that overcurrent protective devices not be located where they could be exposed to physical damage. Installing a panel in an area subject to impacts, vehicular traffic, or other physical hazards could damage the enclosure and the protective devices, defeating their purpose and creating safety hazards. Protected locations or equipment rated for physical damage must be selected instead.

questions.question: Per NEC 240.24(E), in a multi-unit dwelling, where must the overcurrent protective device for each dwelling unit be located?
choices: In a central electrical room accessible to building maintenance personnel only
In each dwelling unit or in a location accessible only to the occupant of that dwelling unit
In the basement or utility room shared by all tenants
At the main service entrance for all units
questions.answer: In each dwelling unit or in a location accessible only to the occupant of that dwelling unit
questions.explanation: NEC 240.24(E) requires that in a multi-unit dwelling, the overcurrent protective devices protecting the conductors for each individual dwelling unit shall be located within the dwelling unit or in a location accessible to the occupant of that unit only. This ensures that each occupant can control and reset their own overcurrent devices without depending on others or building staff, and prevents one tenant from accessing another's electrical panel.

questions.question: NEC 240.33 addresses overcurrent protective devices in damp and wet locations. What is the requirement?
choices: OCPDs may be installed in damp locations only if rated GFCI-protected
OCPDs in damp or wet locations shall be in enclosures identified as suitable for the location
OCPDs shall not be installed in any damp or wet location
OCPDs in wet locations must be enclosed in liquidtight flexible conduit
questions.answer: OCPDs in damp or wet locations shall be in enclosures identified as suitable for the location
questions.explanation: NEC 240.33 requires that when overcurrent protective devices are installed in damp or wet locations, they shall be in enclosures identified (listed and labeled) as suitable for the prevailing conditions. This means using NEMA 3R, 4, 4X, or other appropriately rated weatherproof or raintight enclosures to prevent moisture from compromising the OCPD and creating shock or fire hazards.

questions.question: NEC 240.40 addresses the interrupting rating of overcurrent devices. What does this section require?
choices: OCPDs must have an interrupting rating not less than the nominal voltage of the circuit
OCPDs must have an interrupting rating equal to or greater than the maximum available fault current at their line terminals
OCPDs must have an interrupting rating of at least 10,000 amperes for all installations
OCPDs must be replaced when the available fault current exceeds 22,000 amperes
questions.answer: OCPDs must have an interrupting rating equal to or greater than the maximum available fault current at their line terminals
questions.explanation: NEC 240.40 requires that overcurrent protective devices be rated for the available fault current at their line terminals. The interrupting rating of the OCPD must be equal to or greater than the maximum available short-circuit current at the point of installation. An OCPD that attempts to interrupt a fault current exceeding its interrupting rating can fail catastrophically, causing fires, explosions, and serious injury.

questions.question: Per NEC 240.60(A), cartridge fuses and fuseholders shall be classified according to voltage and ampere ratings. What additional feature is required for current-limiting fuses to prevent incorrect installation?
choices: Color-coded fuse body that matches the fuseholder
Rejection features (non-interchangeable design) that prevent the installation of a non-current-limiting fuse
A tamper-resistant screw on the fuseholder cap
A label stating the maximum available fault current
questions.answer: Rejection features (non-interchangeable design) that prevent the installation of a non-current-limiting fuse
questions.explanation: NEC 240.60(A) establishes that cartridge fuses and fuseholders shall have voltage and ampere ratings, and that Class CC, G, J, L, R, and T current-limiting fuses require rejection features. These non-interchangeable designs ensure that a non-current-limiting fuse cannot be installed in a fuseholder designed for a current-limiting fuse, preventing dangerous substitutions that could compromise the system's short-circuit protection.

questions.question: NEC 240.60(D) addresses fuseholders for current-limiting fuses. What is the key requirement for fuseholders used with current-limiting fuses?
choices: Fuseholders shall be rated for at least twice the ampere rating of the fuse they hold
Fuseholders must be rated for at least the fuse's ampere and voltage rating, and must incorporate rejection features that prevent installation of a non-current-limiting fuse
Fuseholders for current-limiting fuses must be UL-listed for outdoor use
Fuseholders must include an integral fuse-blown indicator light
questions.answer: Fuseholders must be rated for at least the fuse's ampere and voltage rating, and must incorporate rejection features that prevent installation of a non-current-limiting fuse
questions.explanation: NEC 240.60(D) requires that fuseholders for current-limiting fuses have a rejection feature that makes it physically impossible to install a non-current-limiting fuse of the same ampere rating. This rejection feature protects the system integrity: current-limiting fuses are installed specifically to limit let-through energy during faults, and allowing a non-current-limiting fuse to be substituted would remove that protection.
